subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: State and prove the addition theorem on probability.

mark_split.label: Case (i): E₁ and E₂ have nothing in common
Case (ii): split E₁ ∪ E₂ and E₁ into disjoint parts
Combine the two equations and conclude

recall_prompt: Say the addition theorem, then say how the proof goes — the two cases, and which two disjoint splittings the second case uses.
insider_note: The theorem is asked in its "(or)" form as often as by name; recognise both wordings. Most marks are lost by writing only the formula and skipping the two disjoint splittings.

steps.label: State the theorem
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write the statement in full: name the two events, the sample space, and the formula. A formula alone with no words is not a statement.

lines.text: Statement: If E₁, E₂ are two events of a
random experiment with sample space S, then
P(E₁ ∪ E₂) = P(E₁) + P(E₂) − P(E₁ ∩ E₂)

recall.must_convey: That for any two events E₁, E₂ of a sample space, P(E₁ ∪ E₂) = P(E₁) + P(E₂) − P(E₁ ∩ E₂).
accept: probability of E one union E two equals P of E one plus P of E two minus P of E one intersection E two
the probability of A or B is P A plus P B minus P A and B
for any two events the union probability is the sum minus the intersection
rendu events ki P of union ante P of E one plus P of E two minus intersection probability
P of A union B equals P A plus P B minus P A intersection B
reject: P of A plus P of B
heard_as: minus P of E one intersection E two

steps.why: The union counts the overlap twice — once inside P(E₁) and once inside P(E₂) — so the overlap is subtracted once. The statement fixes exactly what is to be proved.
common_mistakes: Writing P(E₁ ∪ E₂) = P(E₁) + P(E₂) with no minus term — that is only the disjoint case.
Writing the formula with no words: no events named, no sample space.

steps.label: Case (i): E₁ ∩ E₂ = ∅
steps.margin_note: Two marks. When the events have no common outcome, the union axiom gives P(E₁ ∪ E₂) = P(E₁) + P(E₂) directly, and P(E₁ ∩ E₂) = 0 makes the formula hold with the minus term equal to zero.

recall.must_convey: That when E₁ ∩ E₂ is empty, P(E₁ ∩ E₂) = 0 and the union axiom gives P(E₁ ∪ E₂) = P(E₁) + P(E₂), which equals the formula.
accept: if the events are disjoint the intersection probability is zero and by the union axiom the union probability is the sum
case one the intersection is empty so P of union is P E one plus P E two minus zero
when there is no overlap the axiom gives the sum and the minus term is zero
disjoint case lo intersection probability zero, axiom prakaram union ante sum
mutually exclusive case the formula reduces to the sum of the two probabilities

steps.why: The union axiom is stated only for mutually exclusive events, so the disjoint case is where the axiom applies directly. The second case is built on this one.
common_mistakes: Skipping this case and starting from the overlapping case.
Not writing P(E₁ ∩ E₂) = 0 before using the formula.
Not naming the union axiom as the reason for P(E₁ ∪ E₂) = P(E₁) + P(E₂).

steps.label: Case (ii): E₁ ∩ E₂ ≠ ∅
steps.margin_note: Three marks — the main case. E₁ ∪ E₂ is split as (E₁ − E₂) ∪ E₂ and E₁ is split as (E₁ − E₂) ∪ (E₁ ∩ E₂). Each split is a union of DISJOINT sets, which is what allows the union axiom to be used on each.

lines.text: E₁ ∪ E₂ is the union of the disjoint sets
(E₁ − E₂) and E₂, so by the union axiom
E₁ is the union of the disjoint sets

recall.must_convey: That E₁ ∪ E₂ = (E₁ − E₂) ∪ E₂ and E₁ = (E₁ − E₂) ∪ (E₁ ∩ E₂), both disjoint unions, giving P(E₁ ∪ E₂) = P(E₁ − E₂) + P(E₂) and P(E₁ − E₂) = P(E₁) − P(E₁ ∩ E₂).
accept: write E one union E two as E one minus E two union E two which are disjoint and write E one as E one minus E two union E one intersection E two
split the union into E one minus E two and E two and split E one into E one minus E two and the intersection
the two disjoint splittings give P of E one minus E two plus P E two and P E one minus P of the intersection
E one union E two ni E one minus E two, E two ga disjoint split chesi, E one ni kuda split cheyyali
use disjoint decompositions of the union and of E one and apply the axiom to each

steps.why: The union axiom only adds probabilities of DISJOINT sets. Both splittings are chosen so that the pieces do not overlap, and both contain the same piece (E₁ − E₂), which is what lets the two equations be combined.
common_mistakes: Writing E₁ ∪ E₂ = E₁ ∪ E₂ − (E₁ ∩ E₂) type shortcuts with no disjoint splitting shown.
Not saying the sets in each splitting are disjoint — the axiom cannot be used without it.
Splitting E₂ instead of E₁ in the second equation and then not being able to eliminate P(E₁ − E₂).

steps.label: Combine and conclude
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Substitute (2) into (1). Write "Hence proved" only after the formula appears in exactly the stated form.

lines.text: P(E₁ ∪ E₂) = P(E₁) − P(E₁ ∩ E₂) + P(E₂)
∴ P(E₁ ∪ E₂) = P(E₁) + P(E₂) − P(E₁ ∩ E₂)

recall.must_convey: That substituting P(E₁ − E₂) from the second equation into the first gives P(E₁ ∪ E₂) = P(E₁) + P(E₂) − P(E₁ ∩ E₂).
accept: substitute equation two in equation one to get P of union equals P E one plus P E two minus P of intersection
put P of E one minus E two from the second equation into the first and the theorem follows
eliminate P of E one minus E two between the two equations
rendu equations combine cheste P of union equals P E one plus P E two minus intersection vasthundi
replace the difference term and the addition formula comes out

steps.why: The shared piece P(E₁ − E₂) is not something the question gives; eliminating it is the reason for writing two equations.
common_mistakes: Stopping at equation (1) and (2) without substituting.
Writing the final line with a plus sign before P(E₁ ∩ E₂).
